entities.summary:
Berthold of Andechs, a scion of the powerful Bavarian House of Andechs-Merania, navigated the complex power dynamics of Central Europe and the Mediterranean during the first half of the 13th century, serving simultaneously as Count of Andechs from 1204, Archbishop of Kalocsa from 1206, and later as Patriarch of Aquileia from 1218 until his death on May 30, 1251. His career epitomized the entanglement of secular and ecclesiastical authority characteristic of the high medieval period, marked by significant political influence, military engagement, and familial ties to several European royal houses, including Hungary and France.

Berthold's early career was defined by his ascent through the Hungarian hierarchy, largely due to the influence of his sister Gertrude, Queen of Hungary. However, his perceived avarice and the favoritism shown to his family contributed to the assassination of Queen Gertrude in 1213, forcing Berthold to flee Hungary. Rehabilitated, he participated in the Fifth Crusade (1217–1221) alongside King Andrew II of Hungary, demonstrating his continued military and diplomatic engagement. His transfer to the Patriarchate of Aquileia in 1218 marked a shift to a volatile border region, where he governed a vast territory encompassing parts of modern-day Italy, Slovenia, and Croatia, frequently clashing with Venice and local communes like Treviso and Padua over territorial and economic control.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Berthold's long and influential tenure as Patriarch of Aquileia transformed the region into a powerful ecclesiastical principality, shaping the political and territorial development of northeastern Italy and the Adriatic for centuries. His career also exemplifies the complex interplay of secular and religious power during the High Middle Ages.
